text.p: The mark erased early gains on its European cross rates here and retreated in afternoon trade as the latest German economic data threw cold water on recent talk that higher German interest rates are due in the months ahead.
Both German and European bonds surged, with Italian and French bond futures setting fresh contract highs, while the Euromark interest rate futures contracts also bounced back.

The buoyant debt markets were aided by news that Russian President Boris Yeltsin's seven-hour heart operation was a success. Relaxed U.S. markets on U.S. election day also underpinned both the dollar and global market sentiment.
"As far as we're concerned the bias is still toward further German easing, possibly early next year," said Ian Gunner, international economist at Chase Investment Bank.
"There has been a recovery this year in the German economy but it has been from very poor levels and is almost entirely export based."

The easing of interest rate gloom today was fueled by news of a sharp 3.6 percent drop in September new manufacturing orders, reinforcing the unexpected drop in September industrial output reported on Monday. The picture bodes ill for the release of October German unemployment data early Thursday.
"German manufacturing orders came out much softer than expected and will tend to keep a cap on the upside for the mark," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economic adviser at Bank of America in London.

Adding to the picture of sluggish German activity was the DIHT Chambers of Commerce economic report which forecast a modest 1.0 percent growth in the economy this year and between 1.5 and 2.0 percent next year. These are below the forecasts of the German government and private market economists.
Analysts said that because the German recovery is export- led, a significantly stronger mark could well snuff it out.
The Bundesbank's policy-making central council meets Thursday. No change in interest rates is currently expected.

At 1600 GMT, mark/French franc was trading at 3.3785/90 compared with 3.3816/20 late Monday. Mark/lira was at 1002.65/95 versus 1003.60/4.00, while mark/peseta was at 84.14/15 compared with 84.23/25 late yesterday.

The peseta received a sharp boost from the second day of this week's Franco-Spanish summit in Madrid. French president Jacques Chirac said he had "no doubt" that Spain would be ready to join EMU in 1999. Both Chirac and Spanish Prime Minister Jose-Maria Aznar said they hoped Italy will be there too.
Chirac also said he expected talks on the lira's return to the European exchange rate mechanism to end by year-end.
The lira got an independent boost later in the day after the lower house of the Italian parliament approved the first article of the government's proposed 1997 budget.

Analysts expect that ERM entry will take place, most likely with a central rate at 1,000 per mark, once the 70 budget articles are passed. Treasury Minister Carlo Ciampi said at the weekend that an ERM return could be as soon as mid-November.
The European Union's powerful monetary committee meets tomorrow for two days.
Elsewhere, the Norwegian central bank unexpectedly cut its key overnight lending rate to 6.0 percent from 6.5 percent in order to cap the recent sharp rise of the Norwegian crown.
The crown, which set its highest level in almost four years at 4.1910 per mark today, ended the day little chganged from the opening at 4.2015.
Tomorrow, traders will keep a close eye on dollar/mark after the results of the U.S. presidential and congressional elections come in overnight. President Bill Clinton is expected to retain office.
--Mike Dolan, London Newsroom +44 171 542 6762
